newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Drought-hit Ethiopian region appeals for aid.
newsitem.headline: Drought-hit Ethiopian region appeals for aid.

text.p: Ethiopia's Somali regional state in the east has declared a state of emergency and appealed for international food aid for its starving people and animals.

But the U.N. World Food Programme (WFP) said on Friday that "in a remarkable turnabout, Ethiopia has gone from being a drought victim to a surplus producer of grain, some of which has been purchased by WFP to assist drought victims in Kenya".
Ethiopian television said on Thursday the Somali region had declared a state of emergency, with 600,000 people affected.
"People and animals have died due to acute shortages of drinking water and many have started evacuating their villages," the Somali region state government said in a statement.

It blamed the drought on the failure of long rains in September and appealed to international donors for urgent supplies. It said major Somali towns, including the regional capital Jijiga, Gode, Deghabour and Kebir Dehar, were affected.

But WFP Regional Manager for the Horn of Africa Mike Sackett said in the Kenyan capital Nairobi: "It's quite significant that Ethiopia is now in a position to export food surplus to neighbouring countries.

"Considering Ethiopia's bumper harvest, it makes good sense to support their agricultural production and at the same time, to draw on available food stocks only a day-drive away," he said in a statement.
WFP said 32 lorries carrying 1,246 tonnes of Ethiopian maize, brought by WFP to feed some 40,000 people, were expected to arrive in the north Kenyan border town of Moyale on Friday.
"Over the coming weeks, WFP plans to purchase 5,233 tonnes of maize from Ethiopia, plus 950 tonnes of beans," it said.

On Wednesday, the U.N. food agency FAO said despite an increase of 20 percent in 1996 cereal and pulse production, some 1.9 million Ethiopians would need food assistance in 1997. FAO said a number of Ethiopian regions faced food shortages.

"In the chronically food insecure zones of Tigray, Wollo, Waghamra and North Oromo, despite a substantial increase in food production this year, sizeable sections of the population are unable to produce enough food due to their poor resource base and the lack of other income earning opportunities," FAO said.
"Overall, however, a bumper cereal has been gathered and donors are urged to support the purchases and movement of local surpluses to deficit areas," FAO said in a crop status report.

FAO said in Eritrea, a former Ethiopian province that won independence in 1993, cereal and pulses harvests in 1996 were cut by dry weather in mid-season. It said production was expected to be lower than last year's and well below average.
FAO said it also saw a need for food assistance for Eritrea in 1997.
